title: Payback Period
subtitle: How long does it take to recover the initial investment?
openingQuestion: Invest 500 million, profit 100 million/year. What is the payback period?
explanation: Payback period counts the number of years until cumulative cash flow equals the initial outlay. Its advantage is that it's easy to understand and says something NPV doesn't: how long capital stays tied up. But it has two serious flaws - it ignores the time value of money, and it's completely blind to everything that happens after the payback date. A project that pays back in three years and then stops earning would rank above one that pays back in four years and then keeps earning for twenty more.

diagram.label: The year cumulative cash equals the outlay is payback
Ignores the time value of money and everything after that

realWorldExample.description: Many manufacturers still use Payback Period as a quick initial screening criterion before moving to a more detailed NPV/IRR analysis - especially useful for assessing liquidity risk when the initial capital outlay is large and needs to be recovered quickly in an uncertain business environment.

quiz.question: How does Discounted Payback Period differ from the ordinary Payback Period?
options: It adds the asset's salvage value at the end of its life
It only counts cash flows in the years after the payback point
It discounts the cash flow before accumulating it
It's calculated on accounting profit instead of cash flow
quiz.explanation: Discounted Payback Period discounts cash flows to present value before accumulating toward payback → always longer than the ordinary Payback. Better than the ordinary version but still ignores cash flow after the payback point.

quiz.question: Why do many companies in emerging markets or industries with high policy risk still prioritize Payback Period despite knowing its theoretical limits relative to NPV?
options: Because regulators require reporting on this metric
Because NPV doesn't apply in emerging markets
Because Payback gives more accurate results under high inflation
Because exposure time to risk is a genuine concern
quiz.explanation: Even though NPV is theoretically superior in finance, Payback Period still has real practical value as an additional liquidity risk indicator - especially important in markets with high policy or macroeconomic uncertainty, where 'time exposed to risk' matters beyond pure expected value.

quiz.question: Invest 500 million, level cash flow of 100 million/year. What is the Payback Period?
options: 5 years (= 500 ÷ 100 per year)
0.2 years (= 100 ÷ 500, inverting numerator and denominator)
10 years (= 500 ÷ 50, using half the actual annual cash flow by mistake)
6 years (= 500 ÷ 100, then add one)
quiz.explanation: Payback = Investment / Annual cash flow = 500/100 = 5 years. This figure doesn't yet account for the fact that year five's 100 million is worth less than year one's 100 million.

quiz.question: Same project but discounted at 10%. How does the Discounted Payback change?
options: Still exactly 5 years since total cash flow hasn't changed
Stretches to about 7.3 years because each cash flow shrinks
Shortens to about 4 years thanks to a higher present value
Can't be calculated without knowing the ending salvage value
quiz.explanation: Accumulating PV: by year 5 you're only at 379 million, by year 7 you're at 487 million, hitting 500 in year eight. If the investment committee has a 6-year approval threshold, the two methods give opposite conclusions on the exact same project.

quiz.question: Two projects both have a Payback of 5 years: A generates additional cash flow for 10 more years, B stops right after payback. What does Payback tell you?
options: Ranks B higher because it recovers capital cleanly and finishes
Ranks A higher because A's total cash flow is much larger
Can't distinguish them - it stops counting at that point
Can't be compared without knowing each project's capital scale
quiz.explanation: This is the metric's biggest blind spot: every dollar after the payback point is invisible. A creates an extra 1 billion of value while still looking identical to B on the ranking table.

keyTakeaways: Simple but ignores the time value of money
Good for assessing liquidity, not for measuring value creation

practicePrompt.question: A project requires an investment of 600 million VND, expected to generate a level cash flow of 150 million VND per year. What is this project's Payback Period, and why should this metric only be used as a secondary measure, not a replacement for NPV?
options: Payback = 600/150 = 4 years, but it ignores the time value of money and cash flows after that point
Payback = 150/600 = 0.25 years, calculated as the ratio of annual cash flow to initial investment
Payback Period is the only metric needed to decide on an investment, no need to also calculate NPV or IRR
Payback Period always equals exactly the number of years the project exists on the market, regardless of cash flow
practicePrompt.explanation: Payback = Investment / Annual cash flow = 600/150 = 4 years. Payback is simple, easy to understand, and measures capital recovery speed (a useful liquidity perspective) - but it ignores the time value of money and all cash flow after the payback point, so it should only be used as a secondary metric alongside NPV/IRR.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Simple but ignores the time value of money

application.title: Calculate a Payback Period
application.message: Take the initial capital outlay of a project or expense, divide it by the annual cash flow received to get the Payback Period, then compare it with the NPV you calculated in lesson 88.
application.secondary: A short payback sounds appealing but may miss the long-term value that NPV catches.

sections.text: Payback Period answers a very practical and intuitive question: how long does it take for a project to recover the capital initially invested? It's the simplest metric in the investment appraisal toolkit, but also the most theoretically limited.

Payback Period = Initial investment / Annual cash flow (assuming a level cash flow each year). **Example:** invest 500 million VND in a production line, expected to generate a level cash flow of 100 million VND/year: Payback = 500/100 = 5 years. This means after 5 years, the business has recovered the full initial capital outlay.

The ordinary Payback Period usually ignores the time value of money - treating 100 million in year 5 as equal in value to 100 million today, which is financially incorrect. Discounted Payback Period partially corrects this by discounting cash flows to present value before accumulating toward payback - the result is always longer than the ordinary Payback, because every unit of future cash flow is now 'lighter' than its face value.

left.label: Project A - 5-year payback
left.text: Invest 500 million, receive 100 million/year, and the production line ends its life exactly at year 5. Total received: 500 million. Once payback is reached, that's it - no profit is ever created.

right.label: Project B - 5-year payback
right.text: Invest 500 million, receive 100 million/year for 15 years. Total received: 1.5 billion. The same payback point, three times the value - and Payback Period cannot distinguish between these two projects.

sections.title: How far discounting shifts the number
sections.equation: Discounted Payback = number of years for cumulative PV of cash flow to cover the initial outlay

example.title: Still 500 million, 100 million/year, discount rate 10%
example.calculation: Accumulating PV: by year 5 it's only 379 million · by year 7 it's 487 million · hits 500 in year 8
example.explanation: A 2.3-year gap just from acknowledging that year 5's 100 million isn't the same as today's 100 million. If the investment committee has a rule of 'only approve projects that pay back within 6 years', the two methods give opposite conclusions on the same project.

items: Advantage: simple, easy to understand, gives a quick read on liquidity risk
Biggest disadvantage: completely ignores cash flow arising after the payback point
Other disadvantage: doesn't account for the time value of money (unless using the discounted version)
Biases toward short-term projects, and may overlook long-term projects that create much more value

lines: Payback Period answers 'how long to recover capital', not the more important question: 'does this project create value'.
